Savor a moment of calm with traditional Japanese sweets and tea. 🍵 Kings and Generals historical animated documentary series on the history of the middle ages continues with a video discussing the difference between the feudalism in Japan and Europe during medieval period. Were samurai really the Japanese equivalent of European knights? Both served powerful lords and belonged to privileged warrior classes. But beneath these similarities lay very different systems of power. This Kings and Generals documentary compares Japanese and European feudalism, tracing how warrior elites rose within Japan’s imperial order and across the fragmented kingdoms of medieval Europe. From Charlemagne’s successors to Minamoto no Yoritomo and the Kamakura shogunate, discover how local military power reshaped government. Why did Japanese emperors survive alongside shoguns? How did land rights, inheritance, and military service differ? We explore the obligations binding lords to their followers, the changing status of knights and samurai, and the peasants whose labour sustained both societies. Compare European serfdom with Japanese rice taxes, and see why apparently similar hierarchies worked differently. Neither society stood still as its political institutions evolved. Finally, follow the transformation of the samurai under the Tokugawa shogunate and compare Europe’s gradual retreat from feudal institutions with Japan’s rapid reforms after the Meiji Restoration. How similar were these societies, who really held power, and why did their feudal orders disappear? candidates.title: The Most Civilized Battle in History - Fontenoy 1745
candidates.description: 🎥 Watch 350+ exclusive videos on Youtube ► https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCMmaBzfCCwZ2KqaBJjkj0fw/join and ✔ Patreon ► https://www.patreon.com/kingsandgenerals Kings and Generals animated historical documentary series on the early modern history continues with a video on the War of the Austrian Succession - the continuation of the War of the Spanish Succession, which some historians consider to be the World War 0. At the Battle of Fontenoy in 1745, British and Hanoverian infantry broke the French line, only to find themselves trapped in a deadly crossfire. How did a breakthrough become a defeat?As the War of the Austrian Succession shifted toward Flanders, Marshal Maurice de Saxe laid a trap. By besieging Tournai and fortifying the surrounding villages, he forced the Duke of Cumberland to attack on French terms. What followed was a brutal test of leadership, discipline, and firepower. This Kings and Generals documentary follows the campaign from its strategic beginnings to the desperate struggle inside the Allied Grand Column. Discover why Ingoldsby’s attack stalled, how Dutch assaults collapsed under artillery fire, and why disciplined British platoon volleys could break French battalions without securing victory. With Louis XV watching, Saxe rallied his army and committed fresh infantry, cavalry, and the Irish Brigade against Cumberland’s battered formation. As ammunition dwindled and reinforcements failed to arrive, the Allies faced a terrible choice. Explore the battlefield decisions behind this French victory, the extraordinary retreat of the Redcoats, and the fall of Tournai that opened the way for further conquests in Flanders. Subscribe for the next chapter in our War of the Austrian Succession series. candidates.description: 🎥 Watch 350+ exclusive videos on Youtube► https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCMmaBzfCCwZ2KqaBJjkj0fw/join and Patreon ► https://www.patreon.com/kingsandgenerals Kings and Generals animated historical documentary series on the early modern history and history of the United States of America, continues with a new video on the American Civil War Previously, we have covered the American Revolution - the War of American Independence (https://youtu.be/yRfAoxJj5j8) and the War of 1812 (https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLaBYW76inbX5AypzVZ_CMikR68ScB6Is4). Why did the American Civil War begin, and how did the Confederacy lose despite its early victories? This complete documentary follows the conflict from slavery and secession to Gettysburg, Sherman’s campaigns, and the final Confederate surrender. Before the first shots at Fort Sumter, decades of political compromise had failed to resolve the struggle over slavery. Trace the rise of the plantation economy, the Missouri Compromise, Bleeding Kansas, the election of Abraham Lincoln, and the decisions that broke the Union. Then follow the armies across the eastern and western theaters. First Bull Run destroys hopes of a short war. Grant’s victories at Forts Henry and Donelson open the road into Tennessee, while Shiloh reveals the conflict’s devastating scale. Jackson’s Shenandoah campaign, McClellan’s advance on Richmond, and Lee’s counteroffensives bring the war to Antietam, Fredericksburg, and Chancellorsville. At Gettysburg and Vicksburg, the struggle enters a decisive new phase. Explore the battles of Chickamauga and Chattanooga, Sherman’s capture of Atlanta and March to the Sea, and Grant’s relentless campaign against Lee through the Wilderness, Spotsylvania, Cold Harbor, and Petersburg. Beyond the famous battlefields, discover the Confederate invasion of New Mexico, the Red River campaign, ironclads and naval blockades, the Emancipation Proclamation, and the importance of railways, supplies, leadership, and political survival. Armies needed food, ammunition, reinforcements, and governments willing to continue. As Confederate resistance collapses, follow the fighting through Tennessee, the Carolinas, and Alabama to Appomattox, Lincoln’s assassination, and the remaining surrenders. Finally, examine how European military observers interpreted the war and what they understood about the changing nature of battle. Kings and Generals connects the campaigns, commanders, and decisions to explain how the Union prevailed, why Confederate strategy failed, and how a war launched to preserve slavery ended with the destruction of the institution itself. candidates.title: Space power struggle: Is a new space race looming? | DW Documentary
candidates.description: Space services have grown essential to our everyday lives: GPS, satellite internet and communications from orbit. Beyond civilian use, space systems are driving military conflict, fuelling a race for dominance in space. The United States is planning a new missile defence system known as the 'Golden Dome.' In September 2026, it officially confirmed for the first time that it had already deployed weapons in orbit. China is rapidly expanding its own space program, working toward its own space ecosystem, including a lunar base. India, the United Arab Emirates, Russia and Europe are also investing into new missions and independent systems. Space has emerged as a strategic arena in the global struggle for power, with competition for influence and dominance extending far beyond nation states. Private companies control an ever-growing share of space infrastructure, led by Elon Musk's SpaceX and its Starlink satellite network. The war in Ukraine offers a stark illustration of the geopolitical leverage that control over space infrastructure can provide. Since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, Starlink has become a central part of Ukraine's communications and defense. The coordination of military operations now depends, in part, on decisions made not by governments, but by a private company. Control of infrastructure in orbit translates into influence on Earth. At the same time, efforts to safeguard these critical systems are adding further momentum to the militarisation of space. While space technology is advancing at unprecedented speed, the rules governing it belong to a very different era. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, adopted under the auspices of the United Nations, laid the foundation for international space law. It prohibits national claims of sovereignty over celestial bodies and the placement of weapons of mass destruction in orbit, but leaves many questions unresolved. Nearly six decades later, nations have yet to agree on a comprehensive framework of rules for this new space age. candidates.title: Inside the Most Secretive Art Empire in History
candidates.description: For more than a century, one family quietly built an art empire unlike anything the market had ever seen. The Wildensteins bought, stored, authenticated, and sold some of the most valuable paintings in the world — Monet, Renoir, Manet, Cézanne, Van Gogh, Old Masters and thousands more. By one expert estimate, their hidden holdings may have reached around 10,000 works, spread across vaults in Paris, New York, London, Tokyo, Buenos Aires and Swiss freeports. At the same time, their catalogues helped determine which paintings the market would accept as genuine — decisions that could make or erase millions of dollars in value. Their secrecy was not accidental. It was a family strategy. Daniel Wildenstein described discretion as something elevated almost to silence, while the business built enormous power by holding masterpieces for decades and revealing as little as possible about what it actually owned. Then the system began to crack. French police entered the basement of the family’s Paris mansion and found hundreds of artworks stored without a complete inventory. Around thirty pieces were removed by investigators, including works that had previously been reported missing or stolen. Some had connections to Jewish families whose collections were looted during the Second World War. But this documentary is not only about a secret vault. It is the story of how one dynasty became both a dominant force in the art market and one of its most powerful arbiters of authenticity; how hidden inventories, private trusts, freeports, inheritance disputes and decades-old missing artworks became entangled; and how two women inside the family eventually forced parts of the empire into the open. From Nazi-era provenance battles and missing Manets to offshore trusts, billion-dollar collections, secret warehouses and a widow who had lived beside one of the richest art dealers in the world without ever seeing a bank statement, this is the story of the most secretive art empire in history. #ArtWorld #Wildenstein #ArtHistory #TrueCrime #Documentary #FineArt #BuiltOnLies

candidates.description: Lion's Most Dangerous Battles for Survival in Serengeti | FULL EPISODE | Wildlife Documentary Across the Serengeti, lions face some of the most dangerous battles of their lives. They may rule the open plains as powerful apex predators, but survival is never guaranteed. Every hunt, territorial challenge, and encounter with dangerous prey can push even the strongest lions to their limits. During the Great Migration, vast herds of wildebeest move through lion territory, creating valuable hunting opportunities but also serious risks. A lion must isolate its target, choose the right moment to attack, and avoid the horns and collective defense of the herd. One mistake can turn a hunt for food into a dangerous battle for survival. The challenge becomes even greater near the rivers. Crocodiles dominate the water, while lions are forced to leave the terrain where they hold the advantage. A tense lion vs crocodile encounter reveals how quickly one of Africa’s most powerful land predators can become vulnerable when it enters another hunter’s territory. Even successful hunters must constantly adapt. Speed, strength, and experience matter, but timing and judgment often determine whether a lion secures its next meal or walks away injured and empty-handed. candidates.title: The Red and The Grey Matter: New Architecture in Africa
candidates.description: It is a milestone for new architecture in Africa: The new Goethe-Institut in Dakar. It was designed by pioneer Francis Kéré, the first architect from sub-Saharan Africa to win the prestigious Pritzker Prize. Kéré selected red clay for its construction, drawing on local traditional building methods and reinterpreting them for a modern context. An entire generation of young architects — among them Nzinga Mboup and Nicolas Rondet of Dakar-based firm Worofila — is spurring that momentum on. Through his company Elementerre, engineer Doudou Deme produced the bricks made from West Africa’s red earth for the Goethe-Institut Dakar. Red brick could well be the building material of the future: Sustainable, sourced on-site and a naturally cooling material in a time when temperatures are on the rise. They offer a climate-friendly alternative to grey concrete, the dominant construction material of recent decades, which drives greenhouse gas emissions and accelerates global warming. It means the new Goethe-Institut Dakar is more than a meeting place, it's a testimony to modern earthen architecture. The future of architecture may well be born in Africa. Over the course of seven years — years which saw their share of political upheaval — this 56-minute co-production by DW and the Goethe-Institut follows the construction of the new Goethe-Institut in Dakar. It also documents a broader shift that's placing African building practices at the heart of the architectural discourse. King Ludwig II of Bavaria wanted the castle to be a world in which he could escape the realities of being a monarch. And nothing would stand in the way of him realizing his vision. The young king's idea to build his castle on a steep mountain peak was ambitious in itself. Inspired by German folk legends and the works of composer Richard Wagner, Ludwig oversaw every aspect of the construction, down to the smallest detail. Nothing happened without the king's personal approval. This posed an immense challenge for the architects, who constantly had to adapt their plans. But the result is a breathtaking achievement, a highly detailed and consciously historicized architectural feat. And yet what makes Neuschwanstein so special is not the building's splendor, which is often described as kitsch, but the way in which it reflects Ludwig's own idealized worldview. It was intended not as a seat of power but as a private refuge, a ruler's personal fantasy rendered in stone. As time went on, Ludwig withdrew further and further into seclusion. candidates.title: Mark Twain - The Eternal Optimist?   Biographical Documentary
candidates.description: One of the best loved writers of all time, Mark Twain, had a tough childhood in rural Missouri and had to leave school at the age of 12 after his father died. He worked as a printer and then a Mississippi steamboat pilot before heading out west to try his luck as a silver miner in Nevada, where he found his true vocation as a writer. His colourful descriptions of a new and evolving nation and the rollicking tales of his travels around the globe are full of his irrepressible humour, but late in life his optimism deserted him when he faced financial ruin and lost his wife and two of his daughters. His writing turned darker, and he developed a strange fascination with teenage girls. In this expanded biographical documentary about one of America’s most beguiling characters, Prof Yorston explores whether Mark Twain, the eternal optimist, became a bitter and twisted old man as some have suggested, or retained the cheery, light-hearted persona that produced the books that have entertained and enchanted millions for over 150 years. Did he remain the witty humourist to the end did he feel his life had simply dragged on too long? candidates.title: Fall Asleep to the Life and Philosophy of Plato Full Documentary
candidates.description: Plato didn't just ask questions — he changed the way humanity thinks forever. Born into Athens' most powerful aristocratic family, Plato watched his beloved teacher Socrates condemned to death by a democratic jury for the crime of asking questions. That moment shattered his world — and sparked a 50-year obsession with a single question: What is justice? From the chaos of the Peloponnesian War to the founding of the world's first university, from the courts of a Sicilian tyrant to the eternal ideas that still shape science, politics, and religion today — this is the full story of the philosopher who built the foundation of Western thought.
